title: Puertos y protocolos
description: Well-known ports that show up in SY0-701 scenarios, with the secure replacement to pick when a question asks you to harden or replace a protocol.
rows: Cleartext credentials and data. Replace with SFTP (22) or FTPS (explicit TLS on 21, implicit on 989/990).
Encrypted remote shell and file transfer. The secure answer when replacing Telnet, rlogin, or FTP.
Cleartext remote shell. Disable and use SSH.
Mail relay between servers; STARTTLS adds opportunistic encryption. Clients should submit on 587 or 465.
Cisco AAA for device administration; encrypts the entire payload (RADIUS only hides the password).
UDP for normal queries, TCP for zone transfers and large responses. DNSSEC adds integrity; DNS over TLS uses 853, DNS over HTTPS uses 443.
No authentication; rogue DHCP servers enable on-path attacks. Mitigate with DHCP snooping.
No authentication or encryption; used for device configs and PXE boot. Restrict to management networks.
Cleartext web. Redirect to HTTPS on 443 and use HSTS.
Ticket-based authentication in Active Directory. Requires synchronized clocks (NTP).
Cleartext mail retrieval. Use POP3S on 995.
Time sync for log correlation and Kerberos. Unsecured NTP servers can be abused for amplification.
Windows remote procedure calls; should never be exposed to the internet.
Legacy Windows networking; disable where possible and block at the perimeter.
Cleartext mail retrieval that keeps mail on the server. Use IMAPS on 993.
v1/v2c send community strings in cleartext. Use SNMPv3 for authentication and encryption.
Directory queries in cleartext. Use LDAPS on 636 or StartTLS on 389.
HTTP over TLS. Also carries TLS VPNs and DNS over HTTPS, which makes it hard to filter by port alone.
Windows file sharing; exploited by worms (e.g., EternalBlue). Disable SMBv1, block at the perimeter.
Mail submission with TLS from the first byte.
Negotiates IPSec security associations and keys.
Cleartext, unauthenticated log transport. Use syslog over TLS on 6514.
Authenticated client mail submission, upgraded with STARTTLS.
LDAP over TLS; the secure choice for directory lookups.
FTP over TLS. Not the same as SFTP, which runs over SSH on 22.
Database listener; keep off the internet and restrict to app servers.
Older port assignment still seen on some devices.
No encryption of its own; normally deployed as L2TP/IPSec.
Legacy VPN with weak MS-CHAPv2 authentication; replace with IPSec or TLS VPN.
AAA for Wi-Fi (802.1X), VPN, and NAC. Only the password attribute is protected.
Database listener; restrict access and require TLS.
Windows remote desktop; a top ransomware entry point. Put behind VPN or a jump server with MFA.
Encapsulates ESP in UDP so IPSec works through NAT.
Encrypted call signaling; pair with SRTP to protect the media stream.
Encrypted, reliable log forwarding to a SIEM.
Common for proxies, admin consoles, and app servers; often forgotten during hardening.
ESP encrypts and authenticates; AH authenticates only. Firewalls must allow the protocol numbers, not a port.
